title: Systemic corticosteroids in critical illness: an evidence-based framework for clinical decision-making

Purpose Systemic corticosteroids are pivotal in managing inflammation-driven critical illnesses, yet bedside translation remains inconsistent. This systematic review establishes an evidence-based framework for clinical decision-making by horizontally synthesizing contemporary evidence across severe community-acquired pneumonia (sCAP), acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and septic shock. Methods A systematic electronic search was conducted across PubMed, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library up to early 2026. Peer-reviewed randomized controlled trials (RCTs), systematic reviews, and meta-analyses published in English were eligible. Data regarding population characteristics, dosing regimens, initiation timing, duration, and safety profiles were independently extracted and qualitatively synthesized. Results Landmark trials define context-dependent efficacy: early hydrocortisone continuous infusion significantly reduces 28-day mortality in sCAP (CAPE COD), while a 10-day dexamethasone regimen improves ventilator-free days and survival in moderate-to-severe ARDS (DEXA-ARDS). In septic shock, early hydrocortisone-fludrocortisone combination accelerates shock resolution and lowers 90-day mortality (APROCCHS). These outcomes align with distinct pharmacological profiles: hydrocortisone provides dual glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid activity to restore vascular tone, whereas dexamethasone exerts potent transrepression of proinflammatory transcription factors. To mitigate steroid-induced harm, protocolized safety targets are essential, including maintaining blood glucose at 140–180 mg/dL and actively monitoring for secondary infections. Conclusion Corticosteroids do not exert a uniform class effect. Bedside success requires personalized, protocolized regimens optimized by scenario-specific timing, dosing, and proactive adverse-event monitoring. Severe community-acquired pneumonia (sCAP) [ 2 ], acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) [ 3 ], and septic shock [ 4 ] are frequently encountered in daily critical care practice and often require complex, time-sensitive therapeutic decisions. Although advancements in ventilation strategies, antimicrobial therapy, and hemodynamic support have improved clinical outcomes [ 5 ], these measures alone may be insufficient to alter the disease course in some patients. Adjunct pharmacologic therapy maybe benefits but its role remains unclear. Evidence suggests that sCAP, ARDS, and septic shock all dysregulate host inflammatory responses, causing tissue injury, organ dysfunction, and circulatory instability [ 6 ]. Because of their anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties, systemic corticosteroids have been evaluated as adjunct treatments in these conditions [ 7 ]. However, early trials yielded heterogeneous results. Concerns regarding secondary infections, metabolic complications, and delayed pathogen clearance limited widespread adoption. Moreover, uncertainty regarding appropriate patient selection, dosing intensity, and treatment duration complicated clinical implementation [ 8 ]. The publication of several large randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating standardized regimens and applying clear inclusion criteria has sparked interest in corticosteroid therapy for various critical illnesses. Trials [ 9 , 10 ] have clarified the potential benefits and risks of corticosteroid initiation at specific disease stages and their administration for limited durations. Differences in study populations, intervention timing, corticosteroid formulation, and cointerventions complicate direct comparison across trials and limit the generalizability of findings. These variations suggest that corticosteroids do not exert a uniform class effect across critical illnesses; treatment effects appear to be highly context-dependent, influenced by etiology, disease severity, inflammatory phenotype, and administration timing [ 6 , 11 ]. Consequently, clinicians frequently encounter unresolved practical questions at the bedside, for example, when corticosteroids should be initiated, which regimen is optimal for a given clinical scenario, and how therapy should be tapered or discontinued to balance potential benefits against adverse effects. In this narrative review, we synthesized contemporary evidence from RCTs (Table 1 ), meta-analyses, and international guidelines addressing systemic corticosteroid use in patients with sCAP, ARDS, or septic shock. By highlighting both areas of consensus and persistent uncertainty, we offer clinical insights for personalized decision-making in the management of critical illnesses (Fig. 1 ). Mechanism of action and pharmacological rationale Systemic corticosteroids commonly used in critical care—for example, hydrocortisone, methylprednisolone, and dexamethasone—are synthetic analogs of endogenous cortisol with distinct immunomodulatory and hemodynamic properties. These drugs exert their effects by binding to cytoplasmic glucocorticoid receptors, reaching the nucleus, and modulating transcription [ 15 ][Fig. 2 ]. Although the underlying molecular mechanisms have been extensively described, their clinical relevance in critical illnesses lies in how they differentially regulate inflammation, vascular tone, and stress adaptation [ 16 ]. Corticosteroids suppress excessive inflammatory signaling predominantly by transrepressing key proinflammatory transcription factors, such as nuclear factor-kappa B and activator protein-1, thereby downregulating cytokines such as interleukin-1, interleukin-6, and tumor necrosis factor-α [ 17 ]. In parallel, transactivation upregulates anti-inflammatory mediators such as interleukin-10. In patients with critical illnesses, where inflammatory responses are often amplified and poorly regulated, this dual modulation helps attenuate tissue injury without completely abolishing host defense. Corticosteroids exert clinically relevant effects on cardiovascular function. In severe infections and septic shock, dysregulated inflammation is accompanied by vasoplegia and impaired responsiveness to endogenous and exogenous catecholamines [ 18 ]. Corticosteroids enhance vascular smooth muscle sensitivity to vasopressors and reduce nitric oxide–mediated vasodilation by downregulating inducible nitric oxide synthase [ 6 , 19 , 20 ]. These effects explain the reported reductions in vasopressor requirements, even in the absence of consistent mortality benefit. Among available corticosteroids, hydrocortisone uniquely possesses both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid properties. This pharmacological profile supports its use in septic shock, which is characterized by relative adrenal insufficiency, altered cortisol metabolism, and impaired hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis function—collectively described as critical illness–related corticosteroid insufficiency [ 6 , 21 ]. Notably, corticosteroids vary substantially in terms of receptor affinity, tissue penetration, and pharmacokinetic behavior [ 22 ], exerting variable clinical effects across disease states. Therefore, corticosteroid therapy should be personalized rather than administered as a uniform class intervention in patients with critical illnesses [ 23 ]. For optimal therapeutic decisions, pharmacological principles should be integrated into multidisciplinary critical care management to achieve targeted immunomodulation while minimizing metabolic and systemic adverse effects. The following sections present contemporary clinical evidence and recommendations for corticosteroid use across critical illnesses. To facilitate clinical selection at the bedside, a comprehensive comparison of the pharmacological properties, receptor behaviors, and primary critical care indications of hydrocortisone, dexamethasone, and methylprednisolone is summarized in Table 2 . Systemic corticosteroids for various critical illnesses sCAP sCAP refers to the progression of community-acquired pneumonia to respiratory failure, sepsis, or both, necessitating ICU admission. It is associated with high rates of mortality and complications. The 2024 guidelines jointly issued by the Society of Critical Care Medicine (SCCM) and the European Society of Intensive Care Medicine (ESICM) recommend the use of systemic corticosteroids as adjunct therapy for sCAP in adults [ 24 ]. This recommendation reflects consistent benefit observed under specific therapeutic regimens in high-quality clinical trials. The CAPE COD trial [ 9 ] is the most influential contemporary study shaping current practice. This multicenter, double-blind, randomized placebo-controlled trial was conducted in France. It included 800 ICU patients with sCAP and compared continuous intravenous hydrocortisone (dose: 200 mg/day) with placebo. Both the intervention and control groups received standard care. After 4 days of treatment, corticosteroid therapy was subsequently adjusted to clinical response, with a maximum duration of 14 days and protocolized tapering upon clinical improvement. The trial initially sought to enroll 1,146 patients, but it was terminated early following interim analysis, given a substantial survival signal favoring hydrocortisone. At 28 days, all-cause mortality was lower in the intervention group than in the control group (6.2% vs. 11.9%), corresponding to an absolute risk reduction of 5.7% ( p = 0.006). This difference persisted at 90 days (intervention group vs. control group: 9.3% vs. 14.7%). Furthermore, the rates of subsequent endotracheal intubation and vasopressor requirements were lower in the intervention group than in the control group, suggesting deceleration of disease progression rather than an isolated survival benefit. Prespecified subgroup analyses revealed generally consistent treatment effects across most categories. Although larger effect sizes were observed in some subgroups, such as older adults, female patients, patients with higher Pneumonia Severity Index scores, and patients without an identified pathogen, the findings should be interpreted cautiously because of the exploratory nature of subgroup analyses. Nevertheless, the overall pattern confirms that early, short-term hydrocortisone therapy may benefit certain patients with sCAP. Notably, not all RCTs evaluating corticosteroids for use in sCAP have yielded positive results. The ESCAPe trial [ 25 ] evaluated the efficacy of prolonged (20 days) low-dose methylprednisolone in managing ICU patients with sCAP. Compared with placebo, the drug did not significantly reduce the rate of 60-day all-cause mortality. These inconsistencies may be partly explained by interstudy differences in corticosteroid formulation, treatment duration, and initiation timing. Taken together, the trials suggest that the benefit of corticosteroids in sCAP neither represents a uniform class effect nor increases with prolonged treatment duration. Rather, clinical efficacy depends on appropriate drug selection and early initiation using clearly defined, time-limited regimens. Compared with the CAPE COD trial, which emphasized early initiation and short-term therapy, the ESCAPe trial opted for delayed initiation and prolonged therapy; this approach might have intensified cumulative metabolic and infection-related adverse effects. Moreover, delayed intervention may have coincided with a later phase of pulmonary inflammation, when corticosteroid-mediated immunomodulation is less effective or potentially detrimental [ 9 , 25 ]. Inter-RCT variations have been quantitatively validated by subsequent systematic and network meta-analyses. A 2025 systematic network meta-analysis [ 26 ] of 11 RCTs (2,042 patients with sCAP) compared multiple corticosteroids—hydrocortisone, dexamethasone, prednisolone, and methylprednisolone—against placebo. Compared with placebo, hydrocortisone significantly reduced all-cause mortality (relative risk [RR]: 0.35; 95% Bayesian credible interval: 0.14–0.64) and mechanical ventilation requirement (RR: 0.73; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.51–0.93). However, the other corticosteroids conferred no significant mortality benefit. Although direct head-to-head comparisons among corticosteroids revealed no single superior drug with high certainty, ranking probability analyses indicated that hydrocortisone had the highest likelihood of reducing mortality (surface under the cumulative ranking curve: 88.7%), whereas prednisone had the lowest likelihood. Notably, hydrocortisone did not increased the risk of severe adverse events. Dose–response analyses suggested that low to moderate dosing (equivalent to methylprednisolone < 1 mg/kg/day) combined with short treatment duration (≤ 7 days) achieved the best balance between efficacy and safety. Low-to-moderate-dose regimens led to approximately 50% reductions in both mortality and intubation rates. Higher-dose strategies conferred no additional benefit. Similarly, short-term therapy outperformed long-term therapy in reducing mortality and ventilator use. Taken together, contemporary evidence and the 2024 SCCM/ESICM guideline consensus indicate that the central question regarding corticosteroid therapy for sCAP is no longer whether corticosteroids should be used but rather how they should be used [ 24 ]. Early initiation in appropriately selected patients, preferential use of hydrocortisone, use of low to moderate dosing, and predefined short duration of treatment can maximize clinical benefit while minimizing excessive immunosuppression and metabolic complications. International expert consensus and guidelines support consideration of adjunct systemic corticosteroids in adults with sCAP requiring ICU admission, particularly when initiated early in the disease course. In clinical practice, corticosteroid therapy is generally considered appropriate for patients exhibiting pronounced systemic inflammation or persistent disease severity despite standard initial management. Typical clinical features include sustained high oxygen requirements, extensive bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, or evolving hemodynamic instability. Early initiation—most commonly within the first 72 h after disease onset or ICU admission—may be crucial for maximizing the anti-inflammatory benefits of corticosteroids before irreversible lung injury or fibroproliferative changes [ 27 ]. Regarding drug selection and dosing, intravenous hydrocortisone at a cumulative dose of 200 mg/day remains the most extensively studied and commonly adopted regimen. This dose may be administered either as a continuous infusion or as intermittent bolus dosing (e.g., 50 mg every 6 h), with both approaches considered clinically equivalent in terms of efficacy. This strategy is consistent with the dosing protocols used in the CAPE COD trial and supported by multiple contemporary meta-analyses; it balances therapeutic benefit with an acceptable safety profile [ 9 , 26 ]. Regarding treatment duration, current evidence favors a short-term approach. A duration of approximately 5–7 days is commonly recommended, with consideration for dose tapering or discontinuation once clear signs of clinical improvement appear—for example, resolution of severe hypoxemia, stabilization of respiratory status, or successful weaning from mechanical ventilation. Treatment duration is limited to prevent corticosteroid-related adverse events without compromising efficacy. The rationale for corticosteroid use differs between patients with sCAP and those with sCAP complicated by septic shock. The CAPE COD trial deliberately excluded patients with septic shock to isolate the pulmonary effects of corticosteroids in sCAP [ 9 ]. Thus, in patients who present with or subsequently develop septic shock requiring vasopressors, corticosteroid use should be guided primarily by evidence and recommendations specific to septic shock management, where the primary goal is hemodynamic stabilization rather than pulmonary inflammation alleviation (discussed in the subsequent section). In summary, for patients with sCAP without concomitant septic shock, early initiation of a clearly defined, short-term, moderate-dose hydrocortisone regimen appears most likely to improve survival and decelerate disease progression. Careful patient selection, adherence to evidence-based dosing, and ongoing clinical reassessment are essential to realize the potential benefits of corticosteroid therapy while minimizing unnecessary exposure and risk. ARDS ARDS is a highly heterogeneous clinical syndrome that arises from diverse pulmonary and extrapulmonary insults, such as pneumonia, aspiration, pancreatitis, shock, severe trauma, drug-related lung injury, near-drowning, fat embolism, and transfusion-related acute lung injury. Despite diverse etiologies, ARDS is pathologically unified by acute, diffuse injury to the alveolar–capillary barrier, which leads to increased vascular permeability, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, and impaired gas exchange. Clinically, ARDS is characterized by progressive hypoxemia and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on imaging. Despite advanced management through lung-protective ventilation and supportive care, ARDS remains associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Marked heterogeneity in ARDS diagnostic criteria, underlying etiologies, and inflammatory phenotypes has historically hindered the development of effective pharmacologic therapies with consistent benefit across patient populations [ 28 ]. Because of their potent anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties, systemic corticosteroids represent a potential therapeutic option. The earlier international guidelines generally discouraged routine corticosteroid use in ARDS. The paradigm began to shift with the accumulation of higher-quality clinical evidence. A pivotal RCT in this field is the DEXA-ARDS study [ 12 ]. This multicenter trial was conducted in Spain. It included 277 patients with moderate to severe ARDS and evaluated the effect of early administration of dexamethasone. The intervention group received intravenous dexamethasone at 20 mg/day for 5 days and then at 10 mg/day for another 5 days. By contrast, the control group received standard supportive care. Compared with the control group, the intervention group exhibited a significant reduction in the rate of 60-day all-cause mortality (36% vs. 21%; p = 0.0047), corresponding to an estimated number-needed-to-treat value of approximately 7. In addition, the number of ventilator-free days within the first 28 days was significantly higher in the intervention group than in the control group (mean: 12.3 vs. 7.5 days; p < 0.0001), indicating faster recovery of pulmonary function and earlier weaning from mechanical ventilation. The safety profile observed in the DEXA-ARDS study was reassuring. The incidence of newly diagnosed infections in the ICU did not differ significantly between the intervention and control groups (24% vs. 25%). Although hyperglycemia occurred more frequently in the intervention group than in the control group (76% vs. 70%), this did not translate into an increased risk of severe infections or other major complications. The investigators concluded that dexamethasone significantly reduced mortality and shortened mechanical ventilation in patients with early-stage (< 48 h from diagnosis) moderate to severe ARDS receiving standard supportive therapy. International perspectives on corticosteroid use in ARDS evolved after the publication of the DEXA-ARDS study. For example, 2020 onward, several European critical care societies supported the consideration of corticosteroid administration during the early phase (first 1 to 2 weeks after onset) of ARDS. This evolving stance was further reflected in the 2024 focused update jointly issued by the SCCM and ESICM [ 23 ], which provided a conditional recommendation for corticosteroid use in adults with ARDS, emphasizing careful patient selection and clinical context. Evidence from systematic reviews and meta-analyses has reinforced the paradigm shift. A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 RCTs (1,607 patients with ARDS) reported that, compared with standard care or placebo, corticosteroid therapy significantly reduced the rate of 28-day mortality (RR: 0.78; 95% CI: 0.70–0.87) [ 29 ]. Secondary analyses revealed a reduction in the rate of ICU mortality (RR: 0.67; 95% CI: 0.45–0.98). However, a moderate interstudy heterogeneity was observed ( I 2 = 52%). Six RCTs reported a significant increase in the number of ventilator-free days, with an average gain of approximately 3.5 days (95% CI: 2.6–4.7; p < 0.01) and a relatively low level of heterogeneity ( I 2 = 31%), supporting consistent efficacy in facilitating ventilator weaning. Regarding safety, the meta-analysis revealed no significant treatment-related increase in the incidence of hyperglycemia necessitating intervention or that of clinically relevant upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Subgroup analyses indicated consistent mortality benefit among adult patients, those with non-COVID-19-related ARDS, using methylprednisolone or hydrocortisone. However, no clear benefit was noted in pediatric populations. These findings align with those of a prior meta-analysis [ 30 , 31 ], which employed trial sequential analysis and underscored the importance of early initiation and low to moderate (or moderately high) dosing in achieving mortality reduction. Overall, systemic corticosteroids can improve survival and shorten mechanical ventilation in select patients with ARDS. However, the magnitude of benefit is closely associated with initiation timing, dosing strategy, and patient phenotype. Although concerns regarding secondary infections and other adverse events persist, available data from contemporary trials do not indicate a substantial increase in severe complications when corticosteroids are administered for a defined duration in appropriately selected patients. Nevertheless, given the residual interstudy heterogeneity and ongoing uncertainty regarding long-term infection risk, further large-scale, well-designed trials are required to refine patient selection and optimize treatment protocols. The timing and dosing of systemic corticosteroid therapy for ARDS should be tailored to disease stage and severity. Accumulating evidence supports consideration of corticosteroid therapy during the early phase of moderate to severe ARDS, when intervention is likely to confer clinical benefit [ 29 ]. In most clinical studies, “early” therapy was defined as treatment initiation within 72 h after ARDS diagnosis. At this stage, corticosteroids can effectively mitigate excessive inflammation, improve oxygenation, and facilitate lung recovery. By contrast, treatment initiation during the later stages of ARDS—particularly after the first week, when fibroproliferative processes predominate—is associated with diminished therapeutic benefit and an increased adverse event risk. Regarding drug selection, methylprednisolone and hydrocortisone have been associated with reduced mortality in patients with ARDS, whereas dexamethasone has consistently yielded favorable trends [ 29 ]. These findings may be partly explained by pharmacokinetic characteristics such as prolonged systemic half-life and increased pulmonary tissue penetration compared with those of other corticosteroids. Experimental pharmacokinetic data [ 22 ] indicate that methylprednisolone achieves higher lung concentrations than does prednisolone, reinforcing that corticosteroids are not fully interchangeable in the management of ARDS and that drug-specific properties should be considered in clinical decision-making. Regarding dosing strategies, the most robust evidence is offered by the DEXA-ARDS study [ 12 ]. The high initial dose (20 mg) with short-term taper approach adopted in the study significantly reduced mortality and shortened mechanical ventilation without increasing the risk of severe adverse events. When dexamethasone is unavailable or contraindicated, alternative regimens with comparable anti-inflammatory potency may be considered—for example, methylprednisolone at 1 to 2 mg/kg/day can be administered in divided doses or hydrocortisone at a cumulative dose of 200–300 mg/day [ 29 , 32 ]. However, clinicians should consider interdrug variations in pharmacokinetics and mineralocorticoid activity. The optimal duration of corticosteroid therapy in ARDS remains unclear. In a study by Chang et al. [ 12 ], short (≤ 7 days), intermediate (8–14 days), and prolonged (≥ 15 days) treatment durations all reduced the rate of 28-day mortality compared with the rate observed with no corticosteroid use. Notably, no clear dose–response or duration–response relationship was observed, and extending treatment duration did not confer additional survival benefit. Further dose-stratified analyses revealed that although low to moderate dosing (methylprednisolone ≤ 2 mg/kg/day) significantly reduced mortality risk, higher-dose regimens conferred no meaningful benefit. Therefore, achieving appropriate immunomodulation, rather than dose escalation, is crucial for therapeutic efficacy. The role of corticosteroids in viral ARDS is highly context-dependent. The balance between benefit and harm varies substantially by the causative pathogen, host immune response, and disease phase. For influenza-associated ARDS, multiple international societies and clinical guidelines consistently advise against routine use of systemic corticosteroids. The 2018 Infectious Diseases Society of America influenza guidelines [ 33 ] explicitly advise against adjunct corticosteroids unless a separate indication has been established—for example, acute asthma exacerbation, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbation, or adrenal insufficiency. This recommendation is primarily informed by observational studies and meta-analyses demonstrating associations between corticosteroid use in influenza-associated pneumonia or ARDS and high mortality, increased nosocomial infection risk, and delayed viral clearance. Although these studies had inherent limitations, such as confounding by indication and disease severity, the overall direction of evidence led to broad clinical consensus favoring avoidance of routine corticosteroid therapy in influenza-associated ARDS. This position has been reaffirmed by the World Health Organization 2024/2025 updates on the management of influenza and severe acute respiratory infections, which emphasize early antiviral therapy and supportive care as primary treatment strategies [ 34 ]. By contrast, the role of corticosteroids in COVID-19-related ARDS is supported by high-quality RCTs. The RECOVERY trial [ 13 ] demonstrated that dexamethasone at 6 mg/day for up to 10 days significantly reduced the rate of 28-day mortality in hospitalized patients requiring supplemental oxygen or mechanical ventilation, establishing corticosteroids as a cornerstone of treatment in severe COVID-19. Subsequent trials investigated whether higher corticosteroid doses could further improve outcomes. Large multicenter RCTs—REMED [ 35 ], COVID STEROID 2 [ 36 ], and COVIDICUS [ 37 ]—have demonstrated that escalating dexamethasone doses beyond the standard 6 mg/day does not confer consistent or reliable benefits in terms of mortality, ventilator-free days, or other major clinical outcomes. In the REMED trial, high-dose dexamethasone (20 mg/day for 5 days, followed by 10 mg/day for 5 days) did not significantly increase the number of ventilator-free days or reduce the rate of long-term mortality. Interpretation of these findings is tempered by early trial termination, limited sample size, and potential heterogeneity related to circulating viral variants. Nevertheless, similar neutral results were reported by the COVID STEROID 2 and COVIDICUS trials, reinforcing the absence of clear benefit from dose escalation. Several studies have reported numerically higher rates of thrombotic events, septic shock, or other severe complications in higher-dose corticosteroid groups, suggesting that intensified immunosuppression incurs safety tradeoffs without corresponding clinical gains [ 29 ]. Taken together, these findings indicate that, once an evidence-based standard dose has been established, routine escalation of corticosteroid dosing is unlikely to further improve outcomes in COVID-19-related ARDS and can increase the risk of adverse events. In summary, current evidence suggests that systemic corticosteroid therapy for ARDS should emphasize early initiation, moderate dosing, and a predefined treatment duration. For most patients with COVID-19-related ARDS, dexamethasone 6 mg/day for 7–10 days remains the preferred regimen, with methylprednisolone serving as a reasonable alternative in specific cases. Corticosteroid tapering may be considered as oxygenation and pulmonary function improve, particularly to avoid rebound inflammation following abrupt discontinuation, and early termination should be considered once patients achieve sustained clinical stability and successful ventilation weaning. Overall, corticosteroid use in ARDS should adhere to the principle of “early initiation, appropriate dosing, and timely de-escalation,” with treatment decisions tailored to disease etiology, phase, and patient-specific risk factors. Although contemporary RCTs and meta-analyses support systemic corticosteroids in select ARDS populations, emerging expert reviews caution against overgeneralization of these findings. In nonviral ARDS, the evidence base supporting corticosteroid therapy remains variable, and guideline recommendations may not apply uniformly across patient subgroups. Thus, treatment decisions should prioritize patient-specific factors and be revisited as clinical trajectories evolve [ 38 ]. Septic shock Septic shock is marked by persistent hypotension requiring vasopressor support despite appropriate fluid resuscitation, reflecting severe infection-related circulatory and metabolic dysfunction. Although advances in critical care have improved supportive management, reported mortality in ICU populations remains high, often exceeding 30% [ 1 ]. Systemic corticosteroids for septic shock have been investigated for > 20 years, primarily based on the concept of critical illness–related corticosteroid insufficiency [ 6 ]. Some patients with severe inflammation and persistent vasopressor dependence develop features consistent with relative corticosteroid insufficiency or reduced peripheral sensitivity to cortisol, which may suppress catecholamine responsiveness. Exogenous corticosteroids are administered to improve vascular tone and support earlier shock resolution. Early clinical interest in corticosteroids for septic shock was largely driven by the 2002 RCT conducted by Annane et al. [ 39 ], who reported a reduction in mortality rate with short-term, low-dose hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone in patients with septic shock and relative adrenal insufficiency. The 2008 CORTICUS trial [ 40 ] enrolled a broader, less selected septic shock population but reported no mortality benefit with hydrocortisone, although a shorter time to shock reversal was observed. Interstudy differences in patient selection, illness severity, and study design likely contributed to the divergent findings and delayed consensus regarding the use of corticosteroids for septic shock. Contemporary evidence emerged in 2018 with the publication of two large RCTs in The New England Journal of Medicine . The ADRENAL trial [ 14 ] enrolled 3,658 patients with septic shock and compared continuous intravenous hydrocortisone at 200 mg/day with placebo, administered for up to 7 days or until ICU discharge or death. Compared with placebo, hydrocortisone did not reduce the rate of 90-day all-cause mortality. However, among intubated patients, hydrocortisone use was consistently associated with early shock resolution (intervention group vs. control group; median: 3 vs. 4 days; hazard ratio [HR]: 1.32; 95% CI: 1.23–1.41), shortened ICU stay (median: 10 vs. 12 days; HR: 1.14; 95% CI: 1.06–1.23), and shortened mechanical ventilation (median: 6 vs. 7 days; HR: 1.13, 95% CI 1.05–1.22). Notably, these benefits were achieved without an increase in the risk of severe adverse events. The multicenter APROCCHSS trial [ 10 ] conducted in France evaluated a combination of hydrocortisone (50 mg intravenously every 6 h) and oral fludrocortisone (50 µg/day) administered for 7 days in patients with septic shock ( N = 1,241). The rate of 90-day all-cause mortality was lower in the intervention group than in the placebo group (43.0% vs. 49.1%; RR: 0.88; 95% CI: 0.78–0.99; p = 0.03), corresponding to an absolute risk reduction of approximately 6% and a number-needed-to-treat value of 16. The combined therapy also reduced the duration of shock. When considered alongside the results of the ADRENAL trial, these findings suggest that hydrocortisone alone predominantly facilitates hemodynamic recovery, whereas the addition of fludrocortisone confers incremental benefit in select patient populations. However, interstudy differences in study design, background care, and illness severity limit direct comparison and warrant cautious interpretation. A potential explanation is that septic shock may involve not only impaired glucocorticoid signaling but also disturbances in mineralocorticoid activity; adjunct fludrocortisone may improve volume regulation and vascular tone in this context. With the accumulation of randomized evidence, international treatment recommendations for corticosteroid use in septic shock have become more aligned. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 guidelines recommend low-dose intravenous hydrocortisone for adults with septic shock exhibiting vasopressor dependence despite adequate fluid resuscitation [ 4 ]. The guidelines also acknowledge a potential benefit from the addition of fludrocortisone while noting that practical considerations such as drug availability and feasibility may influence implementation. Similarly, the 2024 focused update jointly issued by the SCCM and ESICM provides a conditional recommendation supporting adjunct corticosteroid therapy for septic shock in adults, reflecting a shift toward broader acceptance while recognizing uncertainty [ 24 ]. Recent meta-analytic evidence further confirms this evolving position. A 2024 systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis of 19 studies with nearly 96,000 patients compared hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone, hydrocortisone alone, and placebo [ 14 ]. Combination therapy ranked highest for short-term survival, followed by hydrocortisone monotherapy and placebo. Although corticosteroid therapy was associated with an increased risk of hyperglycemia, no significant excess risk of gastrointestinal bleeding or severe infections was observed. These findings support a survival advantage with combination therapy, but the overall certainty of evidence remains moderate and interstudy heterogeneity limits definitive conclusions. Available trial data and guideline recommendations support the use of hydrocortisone at a cumulative dose of 200 mg/day, administered either as intermittent intravenous dosing or continuous infusion, typically for 5–7 days [ 10 , 14 , 41 ]. When feasible, oral fludrocortisone at 50 µg/day may be added. Corticosteroid therapy is generally considered for patients requiring vasopressor support to maintain target mean arterial pressure despite adequate fluid resuscitation, rather than as part of initial resuscitative management. Available RCTs do not support delaying corticosteroid therapy for adrenocorticotropic hormone stimulation testing, given that clinical benefit appears independent of adrenal responsiveness. Corticosteroids should be perceived strictly as adjunct therapy and should not replace prompt antimicrobial therapy, infection source control, or appropriate hemodynamic resuscitation. Regarding discontinuation, most trials discontinued corticosteroids once shock resolution was achieved and vasopressors were no longer required. Given the relatively short treatment duration, abrupt cessation without tapering is common and does not cause clinically significant adrenal suppression. Nevertheless, a brief taper may be considered in certain patients depending on clinician judgment, particularly when treatment duration is extended or clinical stability remains tenuous. Safety considerations and adverse events (Table 3 ) Although systemic corticosteroids confer clinically meaningful benefits in some patients with critically illnesses, they may lead to various adverse events that require active monitoring in routine ICU care [ 51 ]. The safety profile observed in RCTs reflects carefully selected patients receiving moderate doses for limited durations and may not fully capture risks encountered in more heterogeneous real-world populations. Infection risk Given their immunosuppressive properties, corticosteroids may theoretically impair pathogen clearance, particularly when exposure is prolonged or cumulative. Of greatest concern in patients with critical illnesses are hospital-acquired infections and invasive fungal infections. In major RCTs evaluating short-term therapy—for example, CAPE COD [ 9 ] and DEXA-ARDS [ 12 ], no significant increase was noted in the risk of severe infections. For example, the incidence of hospital-acquired infection in the CAPE COD trial was comparable between the intervention and placebo groups. The aforementioned trials generally restricted corticosteroid exposure to 1 to 2 weeks and excluded patients with marked immunosuppression. Prolonged ICU stay, repeated infectious episodes, and concurrent immunomodulatory therapy may amplify infection risk. Accordingly, unexplained fever, recurrent leukocytosis, and delayed clinical improvement during corticosteroid therapy should prompt reassessment for secondary infection and appropriate microbiological evaluation. Hyperglycemia Hyperglycemia represents the most consistently observed adverse effect of systemic corticosteroid therapy. By promoting hepatic gluconeogenesis and peripheral insulin resistance, corticosteroids often increase insulin requirements in patients with critical illnesses who already exhibit stress-induced dysglycemia [ 14 ]. Across trials, corticosteroid-treated patients required more frequent or higher-dose insulin therapy. Although hyperglycemia itself leads to adverse outcomes, it is generally manageable with structured glucose monitoring and protocolized insulin adjustment. Current ICU practice commonly targets blood glucose levels of 140–180 mg/dL, emphasizing avoidance of both severe hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia [ 42 ]. Neuromuscular weakness Prolonged or high-dose corticosteroid therapy has been associated with steroid-induced myopathy, which may overlap with critical illness–associated neuromyopathy driven by inflammation, immobility, and supportive interventions [ 43 , 44 ]. This combination can complicate ventilator weaning and delay functional recovery. Although short-term corticosteroid therapy is unlikely to independently cause clinically significant weakness, the risk may be amplified in patients receiving neuromuscular blocking agents or experiencing extended ICU immobilization [ 45 , 46 ]. Accordingly, careful attention to treatment duration and continual reassessment of corticosteroid requirement are warranted in these patients. Gastrointestinal Bleeding Corticosteroids may impair gastric mucosal defenses and increase susceptibility to stress-related mucosal injury [ 47 ]. In contemporary ICU practice, routine stress ulcer prophylaxis—most commonly with proton pump inhibitors—appears to mitigate this risk. Consistent with this approach, RCTs demonstrated no substantial treatment-induced increase in the risk of clinically significant gastrointestinal bleeding [ 10 , 48 ]. Nonetheless, patients with a history of peptic ulcer disease or concomitant use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs warrant closer observation. Neuropsychiatric and metabolic effects Neuropsychiatric adverse effects, such as delirium, agitation, mood disturbances, and sleep disruption, may occur during corticosteroid therapy and can be difficult to distinguish from delirium due to critical illness [ 49 ]. In practice, temporal association with corticosteroid initiation or dose escalation may provide a vital clue. Older adults, patients with preexisting cognitive impairment, and patients receiving multiple centrally acting medications may be particularly vulnerable. Metabolic disturbances such as hypernatremia, hypokalemia, and fluid retention should also be anticipated and monitored [ 50 ]. Although short-term corticosteroid therapy is unlikely to cause clinically significant suppression of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis, cumulative exposure merits consideration in patients who experience recurrent episodes of sepsis or require repeated courses of therapy [ 6 ]. Overall, careful patient selection, appropriate treatment duration, and continual reassessment remain central to minimizing corticosteroid-related harm in patients with critical illnesses. Conclusion In patients with critical illnesses, the safety of systemic corticosteroids depends not on an intrinsic drug property but on the interplay between patient characteristics, disease trajectory, and treatment strategy. When corticosteroids are prescribed for clearly defined indications and administered at low to moderate doses for limited durations, the risk of major adverse events is generally acceptable. However, these recommendations should be interpreted in light of key trial exclusion criteria, such as marked immunosuppression, uncontrolled infection source, and extensive prior exposure to immunomodulatory therapies—conditions common in ICU settings. Furthermore, most data are derived from studies assessing short-term outcomes, such as mortality and organ support duration. Data on longer-term outcomes, such as secondary infections, antimicrobial resistance, and the cumulative effects of repeated or prolonged corticosteroid exposure, remain limited. In routine care, the risks of these conditions are often influenced by baseline infection burden, antimicrobial intensity, critical illness duration, and invasive procedures—factors that evolve over time and are not fully captured in clinical trials. For the aforementioned reasons, corticosteroid therapy in critical illness should not be regarded as a static intervention initiated and continued as per a predetermined protocol. Instead, treatment decisions require continual reassessment based on daily clinical trajectories and objective response indicators. Worsening metabolic control, electrolyte imbalance, secondary infections, gastrointestinal bleeding, or neuropsychiatric changes should prompt reconsideration of dose and duration. Conversely, early clinical improvement in hemodynamics or oxygenation should trigger timely de-escalation or discontinuation to avoid unnecessary exposure. A lack of meaningful response within the first 48–72 h similarly warrants re-evaluation, particularly in patients at increased risk for adverse events. Ultimately, the appropriate use of corticosteroids in critical illness depends less on rigid algorithms than on informed clinical judgment applied in real time. By integrating trial evidence with careful bedside reassessment, clinicians can optimize the balance between potential benefits and harms and apply corticosteroid therapy in a manner that reflects both the strengths and limitations of the current evidence base. title: Lung ultrasound in the critically ill
text: Ann Intensive Care Ann Intensive Care 1590 aic Annals of Intensive Care 2110-5820 Elsevier PMC3895677 PMC3895677.1 3895677 3895677 24401163 10.1186/2110-5820-4-1 2110-5820-4-1 1 Review Lung ultrasound in the critically ill Lichtenstein Daniel A 1 D.Licht@free.fr 1 Service de Réanimation Médicale, Hôpital Ambroise-Paré, University Paris-West, Boulogne, France 2014 9 1 2014 4 232558 1 1 4 7 2013 30 11 2013 09 01 2014 24 01 2014 25 01 2014 Copyright © 2014 Lichtenstein; licensee Springer. 2014 Lichtenstein; licensee Springer. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/ This is an open access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License ( http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0 ), which permits unrestricted use, distribution, and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited. Lung ultrasound is a basic application of critical ultrasound, defined as a loop associating urgent diagnoses with immediate therapeutic decisions. It requires the mastery of ten signs: the bat sign (pleural line), lung sliding (yielding seashore sign), the A-line (horizontal artifact), the quad sign, and sinusoid sign indicating pleural effusion, the fractal, and tissue-like sign indicating lung consolidation, the B-line, and lung rockets indicating interstitial syndrome, abolished lung sliding with the stratosphere sign suggesting pneumothorax, and the lung point indicating pneumothorax. Two more signs, the lung pulse and the dynamic air bronchogram, are used to distinguish atelectasis from pneumonia. All of these disorders were assessed using CT as the “gold standard” with sensitivity and specificity ranging from 90% to 100%, allowing ultrasound to be considered as a reasonable bedside “gold standard” in the critically ill. The BLUE-protocol is a fast protocol (<3 minutes), which allows diagnosis of acute respiratory failure. It includes a venous analysis done in appropriate cases. Pulmonary edema, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, asthma, and pneumothorax yield specific profiles. Pulmonary edema, e.g., yields anterior lung rockets associated with lung sliding, making the “B-profile.” The FALLS-protocol adapts the BLUE-protocol to acute circulatory failure. It makes sequential search for obstructive, cardiogenic, hypovolemic, and distributive shock using simple real-time echocardiography (right ventricle dilatation, pericardial effusion), then lung ultrasound for assessing a direct parameter of clinical volemia: the apparition of B-lines, schematically, is considered as the endpoint for fluid therapy. Other aims of lung ultrasound are decreasing medical irradiation: the LUCIFLR program (most CTs in ARDS or trauma can be postponed), a use in traumatology, intensive care unit, neonates (the signs are the same than in adults), many disciplines (pulmonology, cardiology…), austere countries, and a help in any procedure (thoracentesis). A 1992, cost-effective gray-scale unit, without Doppler, and a microconvex probe are efficient. Lung ultrasound is a holistic discipline for many reasons (e.g., one probe, perfect for the lung, is able to scan the whole-body). Its integration can provide a new definition of priorities. The BLUE-protocol and FALLS-protocol allow simplification of expert echocardiography, a clear advantage when correct cardiac windows are missing. Lung ultrasound Acute respiratory failure Acute circulatory failure Pulmonary oedema Pulmonary embolism Pneumonia Pneumothorax Interstitial syndrome Fluid therapy Haemodynamic assessment Intensive care unit pmc-status-qastatus 0 pmc-status-live yes pmc-status-embargo no pmc-status-released yes pmc-prop-open-access yes pmc-prop-olf no pmc-prop-manuscript no pmc-prop-legally-suppressed no pmc-prop-has-pdf yes pmc-prop-has-supplement no pmc-prop-pdf-only no pmc-prop-suppress-copyright no pmc-prop-is-real-version no pmc-prop-is-scanned-article no pmc-prop-preprint no pmc-prop-in-epmc yes pmc-license-ref CC BY Lung ultrasound in the critically ill The possibility of exploring the lung using ultrasound, at the bedside and noninvasively, is gaining popularity among intensivists. Lung ultrasound would be of minor interest if the usual tools (bedside radiography, CT) did not have drawbacks (irradiation, low information content for radiography, need for transportation…). This review will show that ultrasound can be used instead of CT in many cases. We used ultrasound first in 1983, on occasion in François Fraisse’s ICU in 1985–1989, then since 1989 in François Jardin’s ICU, using the on-site 1982 ADR-4000 devoted to cardiac assessment, in actual fact suitable for whole body and lung assessment and not larger than nowadays laptops [ 1 ]. At this time, although an old idea [ 2 ], ultrasound was not routine in the ICUs and had neglected this vital organ [ 3 ]. Many doctors thought that lung ultrasound was unfeasible [ 4 , 5 ]. For demonstrating that this dogma was wrong, deciphering the artifact code was the easy part, but publishing was the hard one, far from finished. We will briefly consider the elements of this code, then major clinical uses. Lung ultrasound is part of critical ultrasound, defined as a whole-body approach using simple machines, one universal probe, new applications [ 6 , 7 ]. Our priority was to publish lung ultrasound, leaving little time for developing basic fields (search for blood in trauma, venous line insertion…). Seven principles of lung ultrasound 1) Lung (and critical) ultrasound is performed at best using simple equipment. 2) In the thorax, gas and fluids have opposite locations, or are mingled by pathologic processes, generating artifacts. 3) The lung is the most voluminous organ. Standardized areas can be defined [ 8 ]. 4) All signs arise from the pleural line. 5) Static signs are mainly artifactual [ 9 , 10 ]. 6) The lung is a vital organ. The signs arising from the pleural line are foremost dynamic. 7) Almost all acute life-threatening disorders abut the pleural line, explaining the potential of lung ultrasound. Ten signs The Japanese microconvex probe we use is directly applied to the intercostal space. In the BLUE-protocol, three standardized points are the upper BLUE-point, lower BLUE-point and PLAPS-point [ 8 ] (Figure 1 ). In ARDS (Pink-protocol), a more comprehensive analysis includes four stages of investigation (anterior, lateral, posterior, apical). Ten signs are currently assessed. All our studies directly compared ultrasound with CT. The pleural line generates the bat sign, a permanent landmark visible in all circumstances (agitated, bariatric patients, subcutaneous emphysema…). It indicates the parietal pleura (Figure 2 ). The normal lung surface (Figure 2 ) associates lung sliding with horizontal repetitions of the pleural line, called A-lines. They indicate gas (physiological or free). Lung sliding is a to-and-fro movement at the pleural line, spreading below. The M-mode helps to understand that this movement is relative to superficial tissues (seashore sign). Lung-sliding indicates that the pleural line also contains the visceral pleura. Lung-sliding, physiologically more discrete at the upper parts, can be very discrete in pathological conditions. Some filters, especially average, dynamic noise, can make discrete lung-sliding more difficult to distinguish. We usually bypass all filters. Pleural effusion, a familiar field [ 1 , 11 ], became of interest to intensivists only recently. Our short probe is applied at the PLAPS-point, a posterior area accessible in supine patients, locating all free effusions, regardless their volume [ 8 ]. This direct approach generates standardized signs: the quad and sinusoid sign. The deep boundary of the collection is regular, roughly parallel to the pleural line, and is called the lung line (visceral pleura). This draws the quad sign (Figure 3 ). The lung-line moves toward the pleural line on inspiration. This draws the sinusoid sign, which also indicates a low viscosity, allowing fine needle insertion if needed (Figure 3 ). Our definition makes independent of the effusion color, traditionally anechoic: the most severe cases are echoic: empyema, hemothorax. For pleural effusions, sensitivity is 93%, specificity 97% [ 12 , 13 ]. Safe fluid withdrawal is possible even in radio-occult effusions in ventilated patients [ 12 ]. Small effusions can be withdrawn for diagnostic purpose (even if they appear smaller on CT), provided a 15-mm inspiratory distance is respected [ 12 ]. This safety distance allows fluid withdrawal without precise volume assessments, yet rough assessment is possible [ 14 ]. We don’t use ultrasound during thoracentesis. Lung consolidations are fluid disorders and, therefore, are easily traversed by ultrasound. This old potential [ 2 , 15 , 16 ], long underused in ICUs, benefits from a standardized approach. Lung consolidations touch the wall in 98% of cases [ 17 ], arise at any site, making ultrasound sensitivity dependent on the site, size, time spent. Most cases (90%) locate, however, at the PLAPS-point [ 17 ]. In the critically ill, consolidations are nontranslobar or translobar, an important distinction because this generates different signs, each quite specific (Figure 4 ). The sign of nontranslobar consolidation (most cases) is the shred sign: the border between consolidated and aerated lung is irregular, drawing the fractal line, fully opposed to the lung line. The sign of translobar consolidation is the tissue-like sign: it looks like liver. Both signs allow for 90% sensitivity (as explained) and 98% specificity [ 17 ]. Other signs are reserved for difficult cases [ 18 ]. The dynamic air bronchogram [ 17 ] and the lung pulse, which visualizes heart beats at the pleural line through a noninflating lung, can distinguish pneumonia from atelectasis. For quantitative data, see Figure 4 . Interstitial syndrome is a disorder rarely recognized with usual tools. Intensivists don’t devote much energy to its detection, yet this application has basic, unexpected potential. Our updated definition of the B-line requires three constant and four quite constant criteria [ 19 ]. The B-line is always a comet-tail artifact, always arises from the pleural line, and always moves in concert with lung-sliding. It is almost always long, well-defined, laser-like, hyperechoic, erasing A-lines (Figure 5 ). This definition distinguishes it from all other comet-tail artifacts. Briefly, air and water are simultaneously hit by ultrasound beams, as occurring when subpleural interlobular septa are edematous [ 20 ]. Three or more B-lines between two ribs are called lung-rockets. Lung-rockets correlate with interstitial syndrome with 93% accuracy using alveolar-interstitial radiographic changes as reference, and full accuracy using CT [ 20 ]. Up to 3–4 B-lines are called septal rockets, correlated with Kerley B-lines [ 21 ]. Twice as many, called ground-glass rockets, correlate with ground-glass areas [ 20 ]. In the BLUE-protocol, only anterolateral lung-rockets are considered: posterior interstitial changes can be due to gravity alone. Harmonics of modern machines can alter B-lines. The BLUE-protocol can distinguish hemodynamic pulmonary edema from ARDS, COPD, and rule out pneumothorax [ 22 , 23 ] as confirmed [ 24 - 27 ]. Diagnosis of pneumothorax requires three steps. Abolished lung-sliding, long described in horses [ 28 ], is found anteriorly in quite all significant cases in supine patients [ 29 ]. It has a 95% sensitivity (100% if revisiting methodology) and 100% negative predictive value [ 30 ]. Pneumothorax therefore is confidently discounted each time lung-sliding is present, as confirmed [ 31 - 34 ]. Lung-sliding can be extremely moderate, up to the lung-pulse, an equivalent of lung-sliding when searching for pneumothorax. Pneumothorax generates a completely motionless pleural line using real-time. M-mode shows a standardized stratified pattern below and above the pleural line: the stratosphere sign (Figure 6 ). Dyspnea generates interfering movements above the pleural line. Vascular probes are usually used, but our microconvex probe has no drawbacks, plus the advantage of immediate whole-body assessment. Abolished lung-sliding is everything but specific: inflammatory adherences (i.e., ARDS), atelectasis (one-lung intubation), chronic adherences, fibrosis, phrenic palsy, jet ventilation, cardiopulmonary arrest, apnea, esophageal intubation, inappropriate settings, inappropriate probes are usual factors, and frequent in critically ill patients. The positive predictive value of abolished lung-sliding, only 87% in a general population [ 30 ], falls to 56% in the critically ill [ 35 ], and to 27% in patients with respiratory failure [ 36 ]. The notion of ultrasound “false-positives” makes little sense when another sign is added: the A-line sign (i.e., no B-line seen), with 60% sensitivity but 100% specificity, a logical finding: interlobular septa come only from visceral pleura [ 23 ]. One motionless B-line discounts pneumothorax. Too superficial linear probes make it difficult to distinguish B-lines from other comet-tail artifacts (Figure 5 ). Abolished lung-sliding plus absence of B-lines, at the anterior area, in supine patients, is called A’-profile in the BLUE-protocol (Figure 6 ). The third step—the lung point—is pathognomonic [ 35 ]. It shows in patients with an A’-profile, at a precise location, lung signs suddenly appearing with respiration: transient B-lines, lung-sliding (Figure 7 ). It is explained by the inspiratory increase of parietal contact of the collapsed lung. Complex pneumothoraces with extensive adherences will not generate any lung-point. The lung-point indicates that abolished lung-sliding is not linked to technical flaws, modern machines, or excessive filters (modern equipments with time lags may generate issues). The sensitivity is 66%: fully collapsed lungs cannot reach the wall. Sensitivity for occult pneumothorax is 79% [ 37 ], proving that the lung-point indicates pneumothorax volume: moderate if anterior, massive if posterior or even absent. Lateral lung-points correlate with a 90% need for drainage versus 8% with anterior lung-point [ 37 ], as confirmed [ 34 , 38 ]. Some seconds are required for well-trained physicians to determine lung-sliding, B-lines, or their absence—less than 1 minute to detect a lung-point. The lung-pulse is useful for immediate diagnosis of an atelectasis (one-lung intubation included) [ 39 ]. The diaphragm is interesting, but we do not devote much time to careful analysis: locating the thoracoabdominal frontline and its respiratory movement shows where it is and how it works [ 40 ]. Clinical applications of lung ultrasound in the critically ill How can lung ultrasound become a daily tool for the intensivist? By applying fast protocols devoted to acute respiratory or circulatory failure or cardiac arrest, by limiting irradiation, mainly. The approach to acute respiratory failure: the BLUE-protocol Acute respiratory failure is a life-threatening condition whose cause is sometimes difficult to recognize immediately. Initial mistakes have deleterious consequences [ 41 ]. The extreme patient’s suffering legitimizes the use of any tool that expedites relief. Reducing the time needed to provide this relief is the aim of the BLUE-protocol. The BLUE-protocol, performed on dyspneic patients who will be admitted to the ICU, is a fast protocol: 3 minutes are required using suitable machines and the standardized points of analysis. Novices can take longer (this time depends on the simplicity and adequacy of their equipment, of the standardization of their training). Based on pathophysiology, it provides a step-by-step diagnosis of the main causes of acute respiratory failure, i.e., six diseases seen in 97% of patients in the emergency room, offering an overall 90.5% accuracy [ 28 , 42 ]. The BLUE-protocol combines signs, associates them with a location, resulting in seven profiles (Figure 8 ). The A-profile associates anterior lung-sliding with A-lines. The A’-profile is an A-profile with abolished lung-sliding. The B-profile associates anterior lung-sliding with lung-rockets. The B’-profile is a B-profile with abolished lung-sliding. The C-profile indicates anterior lung consolidation, regardless of size and number. A thickened, irregular pleural line is an equivalent. The A/B profile is a half A-profile at one lung, a half B-profile at another. The PLAPS-profile designates PosteroLateral Alveolar and/or Pleural Syndrome. PLAPS are sought for after detection of an A-profile (a pattern compatible with pulmonary embolism) and of a free venous network (a pattern making the diagnosis of embolism less likely). The profile combining A-profile, free veins, and PLAPS is called A-V-PLAPS-profile. Each profile is associated with a disease, schematically, with accuracy indicated in Table 1 . The B-profile suggests acute hemodynamic pulmonary edema with 97% sensitivity and 95% specificity. The A-profile associated with DVT provides an 81% sensitivity and 99% specificity for pulmonary embolism. The B’-profile, A/B-profile, C-profile, and A-V-PLAPS profile are typical profiles indicating pneumonia. An A-profile without DVT or PLAPS (the nude profile) is likely to be severe asthma or exacerbated COPD. The A’-profile and a lung-point is specific to pneumothorax. The BLUE-protocol is initiated just after the physical examination and followed by echocardiography, cardiac windows permitting, restricted to a basic, real-time analysis. Called simple cardiac sonography at CEURF, this approach is increasingly developing [ 43 ]. Space lacks to describe many subtleties. Hemodynamic pulmonary edema generates transudate, a kind of oil explaining conserved lung-sliding (B-profile). Pneumonia generates exudate, a kind of glue, explaining the B’-profile. This partly explains the potential for distinguishing ARDS from hemodynamic pulmonary edema. Hemodynamic edema generates the B-profile in 97% of cases; ARDS generates a profile of pneumonia in 86% of cases [ 36 ]. This is found again in the Italian literature, under the name of spared areas (A/B-profile), lung consolidations (C-profile), pleural line modifications (C-profile) [ 44 ]. Countless subtleties (such as the C’-profile, a C-profile with abolished lung sliding) will be included in the extended BLUE-protocol, a definitive version of the BLUE-protocol, which must be considered as a preliminary approach using simplicity. Auscultation data, echocardiographic data also will be included. Regarding rare, double, absent causes, read [ 42 ]. False-positives and false-negatives are of interest, because ultrasound provided data that questioned a posteriori the value of the “gold standard” [ 36 ]. Let us remind that, more than simple CT (which isolated does not have a perfect discriminatory power for a given disease), the “gold standard” was the final diagnosis of the hospitalization report. Hemodynamic assessment of circulatory failure using lung ultrasound: FALLS-protocol Acute circulatory failure is associated with high mortality. Many tools have been successively used [ 45 ]. Echocardiography is one of the most popular [ 1 ]. This presupposes expertise, suitable cardiac windows, or transesophageal approach. Here, we use a fast protocol again based on pathophysiology. The heart approach is limited to the simple cardiac sonography. The lung approach will compensate for any lack of echocardiographic expertise, considering a direct parameter of clinical volemia. Data for using the FALLS-protocol (Fluid Administration Limited by Lung Sonography) have been published, showing the correlation between an A-profile or equivalents (A/B-profile) and a low pulmonary artery occlusion pressure (PAOP), with a 18-mmHg value occurring when B-lines appear [ 46 ]. Caval vein analysis is associated to the FALLS-protocol, especially in the case of initial B-profile. The FALLS-protocol follows Weil’s classification of shock. It first searches for substantial pericardial effusion (likened to pericardial tamponade in acute circulatory failure), then for right ventricle dilatation (suggesting, in this context, pulmonary embolism, schematically). If the cardiac windows are suboptimal, the BLUE-protocol is used instead. Then, tension pneumothorax is sought for. If these disorders are absent, obstructive shock can be discounted, schematically. Cardiogenic shock from the left heart (i.e., most cases) is defined by low cardiac output and high PAOP. In the absence of a B-profile, such cardiogenic shock can be discounted. The remaining causes are hypovolemic and distributive shock. At this step, patients with the A-profile or equivalents, proving dry lungs, are called FALLS-responders. They are those who can, but mostly must, receive fluids, a therapy common to both causes. The FALLS-protocol per se begins: fluid administration. A hypovolemic mechanism will benefit from fluid therapy, with corrections of the circulatory failure, and unchanged A-profile. If no clinical improvement occurs, fluids eventually penetrate the lung, which is normally fluid-free. Interstitial edema always precedes alveolar edema [ 47 ] and is detected by ultrasound at an early step clinically silent, before gas exchange impairment [ 48 , 49 ]. The change from A- to B-lines indicates the endpoint for fluid therapy. Associated with no improvement of circulatory failure, this indicates, schematically, the only remaining mechanism: distributive shock, meaning in current practice septic shock (obvious diagnoses such as anaphylactic shock or rarities being excluded). This septic shock has just benefited from one major therapy, following the current guidelines [ 50 ], with two advantages. Early fluid therapy in sepsis? Far before the diagnosis of septic shock. Massive? Up to the last admissible drop using pathophysiological basis. The intensivist can now consider that this fluid therapy, generating interstitial edema (even silent), has positioned the heart at the beginning of the flat portion of the Frank-Starling curve. Minute fluid withdrawal is achieved, from hemodiafiltration if already present, reversion of passive leg raising (“FALLS-PLR”-protocol), to simple blood cultures, specifically useful here, with a view to positioning the heart at the ideal point of the curve. If a B-profile is seen on admission, the FALLS-protocol cannot be used. The diagnosis is usually cardiogenic shock, but sometimes lung sepsis. The inferior caval vein roughly correlates with volemia [ 51 , 52 ]. The superior caval vein is accessible to our microconvex probe. Small dimensions, inspiratory collapse suggest hypovolemia [ 53 ]. Questions are answered in [ 54 ]. One cannot pretend that the FALLS-protocol answers such a complex field; it is open to any criticism. A validation should raise the issue of the choice of a pertinent “gold standard.” Physicians can surround the FALLS-protocol with traditional tools. The change from A-lines to B-lines, which defines septic shock in the FALLS-protocol, can be considered as a direct marker of clinical volemia. Schematically, A-lines indicate fluid responders, B-lines an endpoint for fluid therapy, making FALLS-protocol not comparable to approaches assessing cardiac output. It provides a parameter independent of usual limitations (transmural pressures, cardiac arrhythmia, invasive procedures, etc.). One point should be understood: the caval vein is usually analyzed for predicting fluid responsiveness: fluid is given, cardiac output monitored. FALLS-protocol does not search for any cardiac output increase. In the described sequence, the A-profile indicates that fluid can (and must) be administered. The B-profile on admission (or appearing during fluid therapy) indicates that the patient is (or becomes) an equivalent of not fluid-responder. FALLS-protocol provides a static parameter, which therefore can be used at the start (unlike dynamic parameters). Cardiac arrest: the opportunity for technical considerations Ultrasound plays a major role when showing reversible causes. The SESAME-protocol, a fast protocol devoted to cardiac arrest, assesses the lung before the heart, because pneumothorax can be discounted in 2 seconds, with in addition, windows usually available. This apparently futile property influences the choice of equipment. The following section is personal and subjective. A valuable combination may be our kind of equipment, coupled with high-level Echo machines used every time needed, as we repeatedly wrote [ 55 ]. Nowadays machines are good. Each probe is good for its devoted application (vascular, cardiac, abdominal). We just advocate to have, before the current trend, defined critical ultrasound using (after the perfectly suitable ADR-4000) a unit built from 1992 to 2010 which was not inferior, especially in the specific setting of cardiac arrest, and made every step more simple [ 6 ]. This machine that we now use every day is 30-cm wide on the cart (no matter its height), i.e., narrower than most machines, laptops with carts included. This answered to the problem of the economy of room in busy ICUs, ORs, ERs, where each saved centimeter makes a difference. It starts in 7 seconds, a critical point in cardiac arrest (in machines with longer start-up, there is nothing to do but wait). Its microconvex probe is a compromise allowing in a few seconds, lungs, heart, vessels, abdomen assessment exploiting its 17-cm range, revealing reversible causes (pneumothorax, tamponade, venous thrombosis, abdominal bleeding…). It is flat, therefore cleanable, keyboard highlights three basic knobs useful in extreme emergencies: gain, depth, M-mode. Its technology does not filter out the artifacts and does not create time lags. Its low cost was an opportunity for most patients on Earth. Each detail interacts with the others, e.g., our single probe lies on our machine top, not laterally, a detail that saves lateral width. Our main work was to optimize each step. Our slim machine is permanently configurated “cardiac arrest,” which works the same, without necessary change, for routine, daily tasks (venous line insertion…). Some manufacturers begin to build machines inspired by this 1992 technology. Unexpected limitations (dealt with in our textbook, some apparently futile) can suddenly appear at any step of the management of extreme emergencies, potentialized by the extreme stress. An issue is the permanent risk to face unsuitable cardiac windows. If the user wishes to follow the SESAME-protocol, i.e., assessing here the veins (especially calf areas), the cardiac probe should be urgently replaced by a vascular probe. Time is necessary at each probe change (heart, abdomen, lungs…), setting change, not to forget probe/cable disinfection (here theoretical, usually a critical point). Complex keyboards turn into hindrances to novices. Several probes make cables inextricably mixed. Cables lying on the floor favor the risk of a machine tipover when suddenly mobilized. Problems occur when each of these small difficulties is added to each other. For expediting the mastery of lung ultrasound, we advise to bypass all filters (a setting one may call “lung”). Each probe provides fractional data (abdominal probe for pleural-alveolar characterization, cardiac probe for posterior analysis in challenging patients, vascular probe if others cannot show lung-sliding, abdominal again for assessment of artifacts length, etc.). Most microconvex probes found in laptop machines do not have the resolution or range of ours. Machines with lag between real-time and M-mode can confuse young or stressed users. Physicians also should check that their cardiac probes are able to document lung sliding in all conditions (skinny patients, dyspnea, etc.). This section was an opportunity to emphasize the interest of our universal probe among others [ 56 ]. We think each user, even expert, should try similar systems, at least once. Lung ultrasound: a holistic discipline A perspective is holistic when the relevance of each of its multiple element can be understood only if integrated with the others. Lung ultrasound makes ultrasound a holistic discipline, as partially seen in the previous section. Multifaceted tool Lung ultrasound can be used without complex adaptation from the intensivist to anesthesiologists, pediatricians, neonatal intensivists, emergency physicians, and others (cardiologists, pulmonologists, nephrologists, etc.), even out-of-hospital doctors [ 57 ]. The lung is a common target in these disciplines. The signs assessed using CT in adults are found without difference in critically ill neonates [ 58 , 59 ]. The unit is easily affordable, generating huge cost-cutting [ 39 ]. These potentials are applicable from sophisticated ICUs to more basic settings on Earth. Lung ultrasound complements poor cardiac windows: B-profile shows pulmonary edema, A-profile hypovolemia, schematically. Its feasibility is nearly 100%: this vital organ is superficial and extensive, including bariatric patients, where the anterior approach provides basic data. Painful blood gas analyses become less relevant. Attractive tool Lung ultrasound is not really ultrasound (i.e., this expert, operator-dependent tool) for several reasons. Just two signs are sufficient to define the normality (lung-sliding, A-lines). This potential allows us to reconsider usual priorities. Once the physicians operational for life-saving protocols (BLUE-protocol, FALLS-protocol), they can quietly learn comprehensive echocardiography during as long time as necessary. Solution to the issue of growing irradiation All intensivists prefer the least invasive tool, all else being equal. Ultrasound is an answer to the longstanding dilemma: “Radiography or CT in the ICU?” Radiography is a familiar tool that lacks sensitivity [ 60 ]: 60-70%, all fields considered [ 61 - 63 ]. CT has a high accuracy but severe drawbacks: cost (a real problem for most patients on Earth), transportation of critically ill patients, delay between CT and the resulting therapy, renal issues, anaphylactic shock, mainly high irradiation [ 64 , 65 ]. Ultrasound has quite similar performances to CT [ 12 , 17 , 20 , 30 , 37 ], being on occasion superior: better detection of pleural septations, necrotic areas [ 66 ], real-time measurement allowing assessment of dynamic signs: lung-sliding, air bronchogram [ 67 ], diaphragm [ 68 , 69 ]. Ultrasound should be considered as reasonable, bedside “gold standard.” For all assessed disorders, it provides quantitative data (Figures 3 , 4 , and 7 ). Pleural effusions can be quantified [ 14 , 70 - 72 ]. Lung consolidation can be monitored, which is useful for those who want to increase end-expiratory pressure [ 73 ]. The volume and progression of a pneumothorax are monitored using the lung-point location [ 34 , 37 , 38 ]. Lung ultrasound will favor programs allowing decrease in bedside radiographs and CTs in the next decades. Limitations Dressings and subcutaneous emphysema make unsuperable limitations. Exceptional cases provide difficult interpretation, even for experts. Is lung ultrasound easy? Some experiences show high interobserver agreement [ 13 ]. A burgeoning literature, up to a consensus conference [ 74 - 88 ], seems to confirm this accessibility. A scientific assessment of the learning curve remains to be done, not in volunteers (creating a selection bias), but in unselected physicians. Care should be taken to confide training to experts choosing simplicity, although one can practice lung ultrasound with any machine, any probe, any teaching approach. Our work was mainly to provide standardized signs, a major advantage of lung ultrasound, because the risk of wrong interpretations is highly decreased. Review, conclusions Lung ultrasound allows fast, accurate, bedside examinations of most acute respiratory disorders. It enables a pathophysiological approach to circulatory failure. Simplicity is providentially found at this vital organ. The versatility of lung ultrasound heralds a kind of visual medicine, a priority in intensive care as well as many other disciplines and settings [ 89 ]. Videos Videos are available at http://www.CEURF.net , section BLUE-protocol. Competing interest The author declares that he has no competing interests.

title: Tracheomalacia and Tracheobronchomalacia in Pediatrics: An Overview of Evaluation, Medical Management, and Surgical Treatment
text: Front Pediatr Front Pediatr 2282 frontpediatrics 101615492 Front. Pediatr. Jennings russell.jennings@childrens.harvard.edu This article was submitted to Pediatric Pulmonology, a section of the journal Frontiers in Pediatrics 12 12 2019 2019 7 328299 512 19 8 2019 26 11 2019 12 12 2019 09 01 2020 12 01 2020 Copyright © 2019 Kamran and Jennings. 2019 Kamran and Jennings https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ This is an open-access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY).
